lead: A plain extraction column can be tall and slow because gravity is a weak force for settling two liquids. This chapter shows three ways to intensify the job: pulse the liquids in a column, spin them in a centrifuge, or replace the liquid solvent with a supercritical fluid. All three keep the equilibrium idea from Chapter 5.1 but change how fast the phases meet and separate. They appear in nuclear reprocessing, antibiotic purification, decaffeination and spice-oil recovery.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.4 for column flooding, dispersed-phase choice and the mix-then-settle duty of every extractor.

blocks.text: A pulsed column is a sieve-plate or packed column with a reciprocating pulse added to the liquid. A piston, diaphragm or air pulse pushes the liquid up and down. The plates or packing stay fixed; the liquid moves. The pulse shears drops, breaks large drops into smaller ones, and renews the film around each drop. Smaller drops give more interfacial area per unit volume, so the column needs fewer metres for the same duty. Hold-up, the volume fraction of drops, rises with moderate pulsing.

blocks.where: v<sub>p</sub> is the pulse velocity in m/s; A is the amplitude from the mean position to one extreme in m; f is the pulse frequency in Hz (cycles per second). One full cycle moves the liquid 2A, so the average speed is 2Af.

blocks.text: Moderate pulsing raises hold-up and the mass-transfer coefficient. Too much pulse makes an emulsion, lowers settling, and floods the column at a lower throughput. Pulse velocity is the operating handle: pilot tests find the range where efficiency rises without losing capacity. The pulse chamber, seals and supports add mechanical height; they do not add equilibrium stages. Pulsed columns are used in hydrometallurgy, nuclear fuel reprocessing and pharmaceutical extraction where a short, closed column is preferred.

A centrifugal extractor replaces gravity with a spinning bowl. The two liquids are mixed and then thrown into a rotating field. Settling speed depends on the force, so a small machine can settle drops that would take minutes under gravity. Stokes' law for a dilute drop becomes:
v<sub>s</sub> = Δρ d² ω² r / (18 μ)
blocks.where: v<sub>s</sub> is settling velocity in m/s; Δρ is density difference between phases in kg/m³; d is drop diameter in m; ω is angular speed in rad/s; r is radius in m; μ is continuous-phase viscosity in Pa·s. The term ω²r replaces g in the gravity version.

blocks.text: The Podbielniak extractor has a rotating drum with concentric perforated bands. Heavy liquid moves outward and light liquid inward, giving counter-current contact in a small shell. A mixer-settler centrifuge uses a small mixer followed by a centrifugal bowl. Residence time is seconds to a few minutes and hold-up is small, which suits heat-sensitive antibiotics and radioactive solutions. The price is capital cost, seals, balancing and maintenance. Centrifugal force changes settling, not the equilibrium split; stage calculations still follow Chapter 5.3.

Above its critical point a fluid is neither gas nor liquid. Carbon dioxide reaches this state at 31.1 °C and 73.8 bar. Near that point the density is liquid-like, and small pressure changes give large density changes. Solvent power follows density: at fixed temperature, raising pressure raises density and usually raises solubility. Lowering pressure drops the density and precipitates the solute, so the solvent leaves clean and is recycled.

Supercritical CO2 is non-polar, so it dissolves caffeine, essential oils and many aroma compounds; a little ethanol is added for polar solutes. Extraction runs at moderate temperature, which protects heat-sensitive flavours. Decaffeination of coffee and tea, hops extraction and spice-oil recovery are common uses. The solid feed is a leaching problem, so the material balances of Chapter 5.5 still apply; only the solvent is unusual. The equipment is high-pressure, so capital cost is high.

figure.caption: The same feed and solvent can take three routes. The highlighted supercritical route sets solvent power by pressure instead of by a liquid solvent choice.

spec.title: Three ways to intensify extraction
spec.aria: The same feed and solvent can be sent through a pulsed column, a centrifugal extractor or a supercritical CO2 contactor, and all three deliver an extract and a raffinate.

examples.question: 2 kg of ground spice containing 5 mass% essential oil is extracted with supercritical CO2 at 40 °C and 200 bar. The CO2 leaves the bed loaded with 1.5 mass% oil. Find the minimum mass of CO2 needed and the extraction time at a CO2 flow of 5 kg/h. Take 1.5 mass% as the mass fraction of oil in the exiting CO2-oil solution.
steps: Oil in the spice = 2 kg × 0.05 = 0.10 kg. Inert solid = 2 − 0.10 = 1.90 kg.
Exit solution has oil mass fraction y = 0.015. For 0.10 kg oil, solution mass = 0.10 / 0.015 = 6.6667 kg.
CO2 in that solution = 6.6667 − 0.10 = 6.5667 kg. So the minimum CO2 is 6.57 kg if all oil is removed and the exit gas is saturated.
examples.answer: Minimum CO2 needed is 6.57 kg, and the extraction time at 5 kg/h is 1.31 h (78.8 min).
examples.check:
oil = 2*0.05
inert = 2 - oil
y = 0.015
co2 = oil*(1-y)/y
time_h = co2/5
print(round(co2, 2))
print(round(time_h, 2))

traps: Supercritical CO2 is not a gas with no solvent power. At 40 °C and 200 bar its density is liquid-like; solubility is set mainly by pressure and density.
Pulse velocity uses 2Af when A is measured from mean to extreme. If A is peak-to-peak, the formula is Af; read the definition.
In the minimum CO2 calculation, use the exit oil mass fraction 0.015, not the feed oil fraction 0.05. The exit stream is the CO2-oil solution.
A centrifuge speeds settling and reduces hold-up; it does not change the equilibrium tie-lines or the number of theoretical stages.
Mass fraction and mass ratio differ. y = 0.015 means 1.5 kg oil per 100 kg solution, not per 100 kg CO2.

quiz.q: Write the pulse velocity formula for a pulsed extraction column and define each symbol.
quiz.a: v_p = 2Af; v_p is pulse velocity in m/s, A is amplitude from mean to extreme in m, f is frequency in Hz.

quiz.q: Why can moderate pulsing reduce the height of an extraction column?
quiz.a: Pulsing breaks drops and renews the film, raising interfacial area and the mass-transfer coefficient. The same duty then needs fewer metres of column.

quiz.q: A pulsed column has amplitude A = 0.012 m and frequency f = 1.2 Hz. Find the pulse velocity.
A radioactive solution must be processed with very low hold-up. Choose between a mixer-settler and a centrifugal extractor, and give one reason.
quiz.a: Use a centrifugal extractor. Its hold-up is small and residence time is short, so the inventory of radioactive liquid in the plant is low.

quiz.q: State the critical temperature and critical pressure of CO2.
Why can the solvent power of supercritical CO2 be changed by pressure at constant temperature?
quiz.a: Raising pressure raises the density of the supercritical fluid. Solvent power follows density, so more solute dissolves at higher pressure.

quiz.q: 5 kg of spice contains 8 mass% oil. CO2 leaves at 2.0 mass% oil. Find the minimum CO2 if all oil is removed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Pulsed columns are common in nuclear fuel reprocessing, where remote operation and small hold-up matter. Centrifugal extractors are used in antibiotic plants and in hydrometallurgy for copper and rare earths. Supercritical CO2 plants make decaffeinated coffee, hop extracts and botanical oils. Research looks at cosolvents, high-pressure mass-transfer coefficients and the energy use of compression. Search for Podbielniak extractor, pulse column flooding and supercritical CO2 decaffeination.
